lead: A recursive descent parser is a set of functions, one for each nonterminal. Each function chooses a production and consumes tokens while it builds the parse tree from the root down. This design exists because it mirrors the grammar closely: the code for E looks like the productions for E. It is used in hand-written compiler front ends and in small language tools, usually with one token of lookahead so the parser never backtracks.
prereq: You need: 2.2 for grammars, derivations and parse trees, and 2.3 for removing left recursion and left factoring.

blocks.text: Top-down parsing starts at the start symbol and expands nonterminals until the leaves are tokens. Recursive descent writes one procedure for each nonterminal. The body of the procedure tries the productions of that nonterminal. The lookahead is the current input token, meaning the next token not yet consumed.

match(t) checks the lookahead. If lookahead equals terminal t, match advances the input pointer and returns true. If not, it returns false and leaves the pointer unchanged in a backtracking parser. In a predictive parser, a failed match is a syntax error.

items: Call the procedure for the start symbol.
Inside each procedure, inspect the lookahead and select a production.
For each symbol on the right side: if it is a terminal, call match on it; if it is a nonterminal, call its procedure.
When all procedures return successfully and the lookahead is the end marker, accept the input.

blocks.text: The code shape follows the grammar. For E → T E′ and E′ → + T E′ | ε, write E() { T(); Eprime(); } and Eprime() { if lookahead == + { match(+); T(); Eprime(); } }. The ε production means the procedure simply returns without consuming a token.

A backtracking recursive descent parser tries productions in order. Before trying a production, it saves the token position. If a later match fails, it restores the saved position and tries the next production. A backtracking parser can handle any grammar without left recursion, at the cost of rescanning tokens; the worst case is exponential. Left recursion must still be removed first, because the procedure calls itself before consuming any token.

A predictive parser chooses without backtracking by using FIRST sets. For A → α | β, if the lookahead is in FIRST(α), choose α. If it is in FIRST(β), choose β. If one alternative is ε, choose it when the lookahead cannot begin any other alternative. FIRST sets are covered in 2.5.
A → α | β is predictive when FIRST(α) ∩ FIRST(β) = ∅
blocks.where: FIRST(α) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from α; ∅ is the empty set. Disjoint FIRST sets let one lookahead token pick one production. When an alternative can derive ε, the parser picks it only when the lookahead is in FOLLOW(A); the disjoint-FIRST rule alone does not cover nullable alternatives. Section 3 gives the FOLLOW check.

items: Backtracking parser: saves and restores token positions, tries alternatives in order.
Predictive parser: reads one lookahead token and selects the unique production whose FIRST set contains it.
Left factoring in 2.3 helps because alternatives with a common prefix have overlapping FIRST sets.

blocks.text: Direct left recursion such as A → A α | β makes A() call A() before any token is consumed, so recursion never stops. The repair from 2.3 rewrites it as A → β A′ and A′ → α A′ | ε. Indirect left recursion must also be removed before writing recursive descent code.

LL(1) means left-to-right scan of the input, leftmost derivation, and one token of lookahead. An LL(1) grammar has no left recursion, and its alternatives have disjoint FIRST sets, with ε choices checked against FOLLOW sets. The table-driven form of the same idea is in 2.6; error recovery is in 2.7.

Some syllabi call recursive descent and predictive parsing separately: recursive descent may backtrack, while a predictive parser is the non-backtracking version. In practice, a hand-written predictive recursive descent parser is the common case.

figure.caption: Each nonterminal is a procedure, and the calls form a tree. E() calls T() and E′(); the green leaves are the five tokens matched in order, and T′() and E′() return at once (ε) when the lookahead does not fit.

spec.aria: A call tree of procedures E, T, E′, F and T′ for the input id + id * id, with the five matched tokens numbered 1 to 5 and three calls marked as returning ε.

examples.question: Using E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → id | ( E ), trace a predictive recursive descent parser on the token string id + id * id. State the final result and the number of tokens matched.
steps: E calls T(); T calls F(); F sees id, so match(id) consumes token 1; lookahead becomes +.
T calls T′(); lookahead is +, not *, so T′ chooses ε and returns.
E calls E′(); lookahead is +, so E′ chooses + T E′; match(+) consumes token 2; lookahead becomes id.
E′ calls T(); T calls F(); F sees id, so match(id) consumes token 3; lookahead becomes *.
T calls T′(); lookahead is *, so T′ chooses * F T′; match(*) consumes token 4; lookahead becomes id.
T′ calls F(); F sees id, so match(id) consumes token 5; lookahead becomes the end marker $.
T′ calls T′(); lookahead is $, not *, so T′ chooses ε and returns.
The outer E′ calls E′(); lookahead is $, so E′ chooses ε and returns.
End of input is reached; the parser accepts. Tokens matched: 5.
examples.answer: The parser accepts id + id * id after matching five tokens; no backtracking is needed.

traps: Writing A() { A(); ... } for a left-recursive grammar: the procedure calls itself before consuming any token, so recursion never stops. Remove left recursion first.
Forgetting to advance the input pointer inside match: the same token is matched forever and the parser may loop.
Choosing an alternative by guessing without FIRST sets: alternatives with a common prefix may be selected wrongly, so left factoring is not optional.
Thinking LL(1) scans from the right or uses one token per production: LL(1) means left-to-right scan, leftmost derivation, one token lookahead.
Restoring the token position after a successful match in a backtracking parser: restore only on failure, or tokens get consumed twice.

quiz.q: What does match(t) do in a recursive descent parser?
quiz.a: It compares lookahead with terminal t. On equality it advances the input pointer and returns true; otherwise it returns false without advancing in a backtracking parser.

quiz.q: Why does direct left recursion cause infinite recursion in recursive descent?
quiz.a: For A → A α | β, procedure A calls A before matching any terminal, so the same call repeats on the same lookahead and no progress is made.

quiz.q: For E′ → + T E′ | ε, which production does E′ choose when lookahead is $?
quiz.a: It chooses ε, because $ is not +, so the + T E′ alternative cannot start.

quiz.q: On input id + id, how many match calls succeed in the grammar E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → id?
quiz.a: Three match calls succeed: id, +, id. The first id is matched by F, + by E′, and the second id by F.

quiz.q: Why must FIRST sets of alternatives be disjoint for a predictive recursive descent parser?
quiz.a: The parser reads only one lookahead token. If a token lies in FIRST of two alternatives, the parser cannot choose uniquely without backtracking or more lookahead.

quiz.q: Give one difference between backtracking recursive descent and predictive recursive descent.
quiz.a: Backtracking saves and restores token positions and may try several productions. Predictive parsing uses FIRST sets and one lookahead token, so it chooses one production and never backtracks.

quiz.q: A grammar has A → a B | a C. What repair makes it suitable for predictive parsing, and why?
quiz.a: Left factor it as A → a A′ and A′ → B | C. The common prefix a no longer creates overlapping FIRST sets for the original alternatives.
Left-to-right scan of the input, leftmost derivation, and one token of lookahead.

beyond: Not for the exam. Recursive descent is the usual shape of hand-written parsers in production compilers because the code is readable and easy to extend with error messages. Parser combinators in functional languages use the same idea as small functions that consume input. Modern parser generators often build table-driven LL or LR parsers, but the recursive descent form remains common for language servers and configuration formats. Search for recursive descent parser, predictive parser, LL(1) condition and parser combinator to go further.
